stem: Bacteria cannot be seen with the naked eyes, but these can be seen with the help of a microscope. If you have to carry a sample from your home to your biology laboratory to demonstrate the presence of microbes with the help of a microscope, which sample would you carry and why?
solution:
I would carry a small sample of **curd**.

1. Curd is formed when **lactic acid bacteria (LAB)** such as **Lactobacillus** grow in milk and convert it to curd.
2. Even a small amount of curd contains **millions of LAB**; that is why a little curd added to fresh milk works as the inoculum or starter.
3. A drop of curd spread on a slide will therefore show a large number of bacteria under the microscope, which makes it an easy and safe sample to demonstrate microbes.
groundedIn: §8.1 — Lactobacillus and other LAB grow in milk and convert it to curd; a small amount of curd added as inoculum or starter contains millions of LAB

stem: Give examples to prove that microbes release gases during metabolism.
solution:
Microbes release gases during their growth and metabolism, as the following examples show:

1. **Dough for dosa and idli** is fermented by bacteria; its puffed-up appearance is due to the production of \(\text{CO}_2\) gas.
2. **Bread dough** fermented by baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) rises because of \(\text{CO}_2\) released by the yeast.
3. The large holes in **'Swiss cheese'** are due to production of a large amount of \(\text{CO}_2\) by the bacterium **Propionibacterium sharmanii**.
4. **Methanogens** such as **Methanobacterium**, growing anaerobically on cellulosic material, produce a large amount of **methane** along with \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\) (biogas).
5. In **anaerobic sludge digesters** of sewage treatment plants, bacteria digesting the sludge produce methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide.
groundedIn: §8.1; §8.3; §8.4 — dosa and idli dough puffed up by CO2; bread dough fermented by baker's yeast; Swiss cheese holes from CO2 of Propionibacterium sharmanii; methanogens produce methane with CO2 and H2; sludge digesters produce methane, hydrogen sulphide and CO2

stem: In which food would you find lactic acid bacteria? Mention some of their useful applications.
solution:
Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are found in **curd**.

Useful applications of LAB:

1. They grow in milk and **convert it to curd**; the acids they produce coagulate and partially digest the milk proteins.
2. They improve the **nutritional quality** of curd by increasing **vitamin \(\text{B}_{12}\)**.
3. In our **stomach**, LAB play a beneficial role in **checking disease-causing microbes**.
4. **Lactobacillus** is used for the commercial production of **lactic acid**.
groundedIn: §8.1; §8.2.3 — LAB in milk produce acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins, increase vitamin B12, check disease-causing microbes in the stomach; Lactobacillus as the producer of lactic acid

stem: Name some traditional Indian foods made of wheat, rice and Bengal gram (or their products) which involve use of microbes.
solution:
1. **Wheat**: **bread** (dough fermented by baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae) and **jalebi**.
2. **Rice**: **idli** and **dosa**, whose dough is fermented by bacteria.
3. **Bengal gram**: **dhokla** and **khandvi**, made from fermented gram-flour batter.
groundedIn: §8.1 — dough for dosa and idli is fermented by bacteria; bread dough is fermented using baker's yeast; BEYOND CHAPTER: bread and jalebi are made from wheat flour, idli and dosa batter is made from rice, dhokla and khandvi are made from fermented Bengal gram flour

stem: In which way have microbes played a major role in controlling diseases caused by harmful bacteria?
solution:
Microbes produce **antibiotics**, which control diseases caused by harmful bacteria.

1. **Antibiotics** are chemical substances produced by some microbes that **kill or retard the growth** of other (disease-causing) microbes.
2. **Penicillin**, the first antibiotic discovered, was found by **Alexander Fleming**, who noticed that Staphylococci could not grow around the mould **Penicillium notatum**. Its full potential was established by **Ernest Chain and Howard Florey**, and it was used extensively to treat soldiers wounded in World War II.
3. Other antibiotics were later purified from other microbes.
4. Antibiotics have greatly improved our capacity to treat deadly bacterial diseases such as **plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy**, which used to kill millions all over the globe.
groundedIn: §8.2.2 — antibiotics are produced by some microbes and kill or retard the growth of disease-causing microbes; Fleming, Penicillium notatum, Chain and Florey; treatment of plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy

stem: Name any two species of fungus, which are used in the production of the antibiotics.
solution:
1. **Penicillium notatum**: the mould from which the antibiotic **penicillin** was obtained.
2. **Cephalosporium acremonium**: the fungus that produces the antibiotic **cephalosporin**.
groundedIn: §8.2.2 — Penicillin named after the mould Penicillium notatum; BEYOND CHAPTER: Cephalosporium acremonium produces the antibiotic cephalosporin

stem: What is sewage? In which way can sewage be harmful to us?
solution:
**Sewage** is the municipal waste-water generated every day in cities and towns, a major component of which is **human excreta**.

Sewage is harmful because:

1. It contains large amounts of **organic matter** and **microbes, many of which are pathogenic**.
2. When untreated sewage is discharged directly into rivers, it causes their **pollution** and an **increase in water-borne diseases**.
3. Its large organic load gives it a very **high BOD**; the greater the BOD of waste water, the more is its polluting potential.

Hence sewage is treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) before disposal, to make it less polluting.
groundedIn: §8.3 — municipal waste-water is called sewage, major component human excreta, large amounts of organic matter and microbes many of which are pathogenic; untreated sewage discharged into rivers causes pollution and increase in water-borne diseases; greater the BOD more its polluting potential

stem: What is the key difference between primary and secondary sewage treatment?
solution:
The key difference: **primary treatment is a physical process** (removal of particles), while **secondary treatment is a biological process** (removal of organic matter by microbes).

| Basis | Primary treatment | Secondary (biological) treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Physical** | **Biological** |
| Process | Sequential **filtration** removes floating debris; **sedimentation** removes grit (soil and small pebbles) | Primary effluent is agitated and aerated in **aeration tanks**; useful **aerobic microbes** grow into **flocs** |
| What is removed | Large and small particles | Major part of the **organic matter**, so the **BOD** falls significantly |
| Role of microbes | None | Essential: aerobic microbes in flocs, then anaerobic bacteria in sludge digesters |
| Products | **Primary sludge** (settled solids) and the effluent | **Activated sludge**; its major part goes to anaerobic sludge digesters, producing biogas |
groundedIn: §8.3; Fig. 8.6 — primary treatment is physical removal by filtration and sedimentation forming primary sludge; secondary treatment in aeration tanks with aerobic microbes forming flocs that reduce BOD; activated sludge and anaerobic sludge digesters

stem: Do you think microbes can also be used as source of energy? If yes, how?
solution:
**Yes.** Microbes produce **biogas**, a mixture of gases containing predominantly **methane**, which is inflammable and used as fuel.

1. Certain bacteria, collectively called **methanogens** (e.g. **Methanobacterium**), grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce a large amount of methane along with \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\).
2. Methanogens are present in the **rumen** of cattle, so cattle **dung (gobar)** is rich in them and is used to generate biogas (**gobar gas**).
3. In a **biogas plant**, a slurry of dung is fed into a concrete tank (10-15 feet deep). A **floating cover** over the slurry keeps rising as gas is produced. The gas is supplied through an outlet pipe to nearby houses for **cooking and lighting**; the spent slurry is removed through another outlet and used as **fertiliser**.
4. In sewage treatment plants, anaerobic bacteria in **sludge digesters** also produce biogas (methane, hydrogen sulphide and \(\text{CO}_2\)), which can be used as a source of energy.

The technology of biogas production was developed in India mainly by **IARI** and **KVIC**.
groundedIn: §8.4; §8.3; Fig. 8.8 — biogas predominantly methane used as fuel; methanogens, Methanobacterium, rumen, gobar gas; biogas plant structure and uses; anaerobic sludge digesters produce biogas usable as energy; IARI and KVIC

stem: Microbes can be used to decrease the use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Explain how this can be accomplished.
solution:
This is accomplished by using microbes as **biofertilisers** (in place of chemical fertilisers) and as **biocontrol agents** (in place of chemical pesticides).

**A. Biofertilisers** (organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil):

1. **Rhizobium** forms root nodules on leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms used by the plant.
2. Free-living bacteria such as **Azospirillum** and **Azotobacter** fix nitrogen in the soil.
3. **Cyanobacteria** (Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria) fix nitrogen and add organic matter; they are important biofertilisers in **paddy fields**.
4. **Mycorrhizal fungi** (genus **Glomus**) absorb phosphorus from the soil and pass it to the plant.

**B. Biocontrol agents** (biological methods for controlling plant diseases and pests):

1. **Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)**: dried spores sprayed on plants are eaten by caterpillars; the toxin released in the larval gut kills them, leaving other insects unharmed.
2. **Trichoderma**: free-living fungi of the root ecosystem, effective against several plant pathogens.
3. **Baculoviruses** (genus **Nucleopolyhedrovirus**): species-specific, narrow spectrum insecticides with no negative impact on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects.

Thus the dependence on toxic chemicals is greatly reduced.
groundedIn: §8.6; §8.5 — biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Azospirillum, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria in paddy fields, Glomus mycorrhiza absorbing phosphorus; biocontrol: Bt, Trichoderma, Baculoviruses of genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus; reduced dependence on toxic chemicals

stem: Three water samples namely river water, untreated sewage water and secondary effluent discharged from a sewage treatment plant were subjected to BOD test. The samples were labelled A, B and C; but the laboratory attendant did not note which was which. The BOD values of the three samples A, B and C were recorded as 20mg/L, 8mg/L and 400mg/L, respectively. Which sample of the water is most polluted? Can you assign the correct label to each assuming the river water is relatively clean?
solution:
**Sample C (BOD 400 mg/L) is the most polluted.**

| Sample | BOD | Label |
|---|---|---|
| A | 20 mg/L | Secondary effluent from the sewage treatment plant |
| B | 8 mg/L | River water |
| C | 400 mg/L | Untreated sewage water |

Reason: **BOD** is the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria, so it is an indirect measure of the organic matter present; the greater the BOD, the more the polluting potential. Untreated sewage has the most organic matter (highest BOD). Secondary treatment reduces the BOD significantly, so the effluent has a low BOD, while relatively clean river water has the lowest.
groundedIn: §8.3 — BOD is the oxygen consumed if all organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria, an indirect measure of organic matter; greater BOD, more polluting potential; secondary treatment significantly reduces BOD

stem: Find out the name of the microbes from which Cyclosporin A (an immunosuppressive drug) and Statins (blood cholesterol lowering agents) are obtained.
solution:
1. **Cyclosporin A**: produced by the fungus **Trichoderma polysporum**; used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients.
2. **Statins**: produced by **Monascus purpureus**, a filamentous fungus (mould) that the book calls a yeast; they lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cholesterol.
groundedIn: §8.2.3 — cyclosporin A produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum; statins produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus, competitively inhibiting the enzyme for cholesterol synthesis

context: Find out the role of microbes in the following and discuss it with your teacher.
solution:
**Single cell protein (SCP)** is protein-rich microbial biomass (of bacteria, yeasts, fungi or algae) used as an alternative source of good-quality protein for human food and animal feed.

1. Microbes such as **Spirulina** can be grown easily on materials like waste water from potato processing plants, straw, molasses, animal manure and even sewage, producing large quantities of food rich in **protein, minerals, fats, carbohydrates and vitamins**.
2. Microbes multiply very fast, so a small amount of microbial biomass yields a very large amount of protein; for example, 250 g of **Methylophilus methylotrophus** can produce about 25 tonnes of protein.
3. Growing SCP on wastes also **reduces environmental pollution**.
groundedIn: §8.2; §8.0 — microbes grown on nutritive media and on an industrial scale in large fermentors; BEYOND CHAPTER: definition of SCP as microbial biomass used as protein-rich food and feed, Spirulina grown on potato-processing waste water, straw, molasses, animal manure and sewage, rich in protein, minerals, fats, carbohydrates and vitamins, 250 g of Methylophilus methylotrophus producing about 25 tonnes of protein, reduction of pollution

context: Find out the role of microbes in the following and discuss it with your teacher.
solution:
Microbes maintain and increase **soil fertility** and protect plants:

1. **Nitrogen fixation**: symbiotic **Rhizobium** in root nodules of legumes, free-living **Azospirillum** and **Azotobacter**, and **cyanobacteria** (Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria) fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the nitrogen content of the soil.
2. **Phosphorus supply**: **mycorrhizal fungi** (genus **Glomus**) absorb phosphorus from the soil and pass it to the plant; they also give resistance to root-borne pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought.
3. **Organic matter**: blue green algae add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility.
4. **Decomposition**: soil bacteria and fungi decompose dead plants and animals, releasing the nutrients back into the soil and forming **humus**.
5. **Biocontrol**: **Trichoderma**, common in the root ecosystem, controls several plant pathogens.
groundedIn: §8.6; §8.5 — Rhizobium, Azospirillum, Azotobacter and cyanobacteria fix nitrogen; Glomus mycorrhiza absorbs phosphorus, resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought; blue green algae add organic matter; Trichoderma common in root ecosystems controls plant pathogens; BEYOND CHAPTER: soil bacteria and fungi decompose dead organic matter, releasing nutrients and forming humus

stem:
Arrange the following in the decreasing order (most important first) of their importance, for the welfare of human society. Give reasons for your answer.

Biogas, Citric acid, Penicillin and Curd
solution:
**Penicillin > Curd > Biogas > Citric acid**

1. **Penicillin**: a life-saving **antibiotic**. Antibiotics have greatly improved our capacity to treat deadly diseases such as plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy, which used to kill millions; so it ranks first.
2. **Curd**: an everyday food. LAB convert milk to curd, improving its **nutritional quality** by increasing vitamin \(\text{B}_{12}\), and in the stomach they check disease-causing microbes.
3. **Biogas**: a cheap **source of energy** for cooking and lighting, especially in rural areas, made from cattle dung; the spent slurry is used as fertiliser.
4. **Citric acid**: an industrial chemical produced by **Aspergillus niger**; it is useful commercially but is not essential for health, food or energy.
groundedIn: §8.2.2; §8.1; §8.4; §8.2.3 — antibiotics treat plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy; LAB increase vitamin B12 and check disease-causing microbes; biogas used for cooking and lighting in rural areas, spent slurry as fertiliser; Aspergillus niger produces citric acid

stem: How do biofertilisers enrich the fertility of the soil?
solution:
**Biofertilisers** are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil. Their main sources are **bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria**.

1. **Symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria**: **Rhizobium** forms nodules on the roots of leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms used by the plant as nutrient.
2. **Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria**: **Azospirillum** and **Azotobacter** fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, enriching its nitrogen content.
3. **Mycorrhizal fungi**: members of the genus **Glomus** form mycorrhiza; the fungal symbiont absorbs **phosphorus** from soil and passes it to the plant. Such plants also show resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought, and an overall increase in growth.
4. **Cyanobacteria** (blue green algae) such as **Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria** fix atmospheric nitrogen; they are important biofertilisers in **paddy fields** and also add **organic matter** to the soil, increasing its fertility.

Thus biofertilisers replenish soil nutrients and reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers.
groundedIn: §8.6 — biofertilisers enrich the nutrient quality of the soil; Rhizobium, Azospirillum, Azotobacter; Glomus mycorrhiza absorbs phosphorus; cyanobacteria Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria in paddy fields add organic matter; reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers
